question: The manual lists four categories of surfaces that increase your chance of falling or crashing. Which of the following is one of them?
explanation: The manual lists uneven surfaces or obstacles, slippery surfaces, railroad tracks, and grooves and gratings as surfaces that increase your chance of falling or being involved in a crash.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.30, 'Handling Dangerous Surfaces'

question: If you must ride over an obstacle you can't avoid, at what angle does the manual recommend approaching it?
choice_a: At the shallowest angle possible, close to parallel
choice_b: Angle of approach does not matter for obstacles
choice_c: As close to a 90-degree angle as possible
choice_d: Always at a 45-degree angle regardless of the obstacle
explanation: The manual instructs that if you must ride over an obstacle, approach it at as close to a 90-degree angle as possible, and look where you want to go to control your path of travel.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.30-31, 'Uneven Surfaces and Obstacles'

question: Just before riding over an unavoidable obstacle, what does the manual recommend doing with the throttle, and why?
choice_a: Close the throttle completely and coast to a stop before contact
choice_b: Throttle position has no effect on how the motorcycle handles an obstacle
choice_c: Apply full throttle to launch over the obstacle
choice_d: Roll on the throttle slightly to lighten the front end
explanation: The manual instructs riders to roll on the throttle slightly just before contact with an obstacle to lighten the front end, after slowing as much as possible and rising slightly off the seat.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.31, 'Uneven Surfaces and Obstacles'

question: After riding over an object in the street, what does the manual say you should do?
choice_a: Pull off the road and check your tires and rims for damage before riding any farther
choice_b: Continue riding at normal speed; no follow-up check is necessary
choice_c: Immediately accelerate to highway speed to test the tires
choice_d: Only check the tires if you feel a change in handling within the next hour
explanation: The manual advises that if you ride over an object in the street, you should pull off the road and check your tires and rims for damage before riding any farther.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.31, 'Uneven Surfaces and Obstacles'

question: When is wet pavement especially slippery, according to the manual?
choice_a: Only after several hours of continuous rain
choice_b: Particularly just after it starts to rain and before surface oil washes to the side of the road
choice_c: Wet pavement is never more slippery than dry pavement
explanation: The manual identifies wet pavement as providing poor traction particularly just after it starts to rain and before surface oil washes to the side of the road.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.31, 'Slippery Surfaces'

question: Besides wet pavement, what other surfaces does the manual list as providing poor traction?
choice_b: New asphalt with fresh paint markings
choice_c: Gravel roads, mud, leaves, snow and ice, and wet lane markings, steel plates or manhole covers
explanation: The manual lists gravel roads, mud, leaves, snow and ice, and lane markings, steel plates and manhole covers (especially when wet) as surfaces providing poor traction.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.31, 'Slippery Surfaces'

question: When it starts to rain, where does the manual recommend riding within the lane?
choice_a: In the exact center of the lane at all times
choice_b: As close to the road's edge as possible, regardless of debris
choice_c: Lane position makes no difference once rain begins
choice_d: In the tire tracks left by cars, since the center of the lane can become hazardous when wet
explanation: The manual states that when it starts to rain, ride in the tire tracks left by cars, since the center of a lane can be hazardous when wet and often the left tire track will be the best position.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.31-32, 'Slippery Surfaces'

question: Where does the manual say patches of ice tend to develop on a roadway?
choice_a: In low or shaded areas and on bridges and overpasses
choice_b: Only in the very center of open, sunny highways
choice_c: Ice never forms unevenly across a roadway
choice_d: Only on roads with heavy truck traffic
explanation: The manual explains that rain dries and snow melts faster on some sections of road than others, and patches of ice tend to develop in low or shaded areas and on bridges and overpasses.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.32, 'Slippery Surfaces'

question: If you encounter a large, extremely slippery surface that you must cross at a walking pace, what does the manual recommend?
choice_a: Apply firm, continuous braking throughout the crossing
choice_b: Keep the motorcycle straight up, proceed as slowly as possible, keep off the brakes, and consider letting your feet skim along the surface
choice_c: Accelerate quickly to get across before losing balance
choice_d: Lean the motorcycle sharply to one side for stability
explanation: The manual advises that on a large, very slippery surface requiring a walking pace, keep the motorcycle straight up, proceed as slowly as possible, keep off the brakes, and consider letting your feet skim along the surface so you can catch yourself if the motorcycle starts to fall.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.32-33, 'Slippery Surfaces'

question: What does the manual say is usually the safer way to cross railroad tracks?
choice_a: Always turn to cross tracks at exactly 90 degrees, regardless of lane position
choice_b: Stop completely on the tracks to check for trains before proceeding
choice_c: Ride straight within your lane; turning to take tracks head-on at a 90-degree angle can carry you into another lane of traffic
choice_d: Cross tracks only while accelerating as hard as possible
explanation: The manual states it is usually safer to ride straight within your lane to cross tracks, since turning to take tracks head-on at a 90-degree angle can be more dangerous because your path may carry you into another lane of traffic.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.33, 'Railroad Tracks, Trolley Tracks and Pavement Seams'

question: For track or road seams that run parallel to your course, at what minimum angle should you cross them?
choice_b: Parallel seams should never be crossed under any circumstance
choice_c: 0 degrees, staying perfectly parallel to the seam
choice_d: At least 45 degrees, after moving far enough away to make a deliberate turn
explanation: The manual instructs that for tracks or seams running parallel to your course, move far enough away to cross at an angle of at least 45 degrees, then make a deliberate turn -- edging across could catch your tires and throw you off balance.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.33, 'Railroad Tracks, Trolley Tracks and Pavement Seams'

question: What does the manual say about the uneasy, wandering feeling that can occur when riding over rain grooves or bridge gratings?
choice_a: It is generally not hazardous -- relax, maintain a steady speed, and ride straight across
choice_b: It always indicates a serious mechanical failure requiring an immediate stop
choice_c: It should be corrected by crossing the grooves at a sharp angle
choice_d: It means the tires have already gone flat
explanation: The manual explains that the uneasy, wandering feeling from riding over rain grooves or bridge gratings is generally not hazardous, and riders should relax, maintain a steady speed, and ride straight across.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.33, 'Grooves and Gratings'

question: Why does the manual warn against crossing grooves or gratings at an angle?
choice_a: Crossing at an angle is always the safest way to cross grooves
choice_b: Crossing at an angle forces riders to zigzag to stay in the lane, which is far more hazardous than the wandering feeling of crossing straight
choice_c: There is no difference between crossing straight and at an angle
choice_d: Angled crossing is required by law on all bridges
explanation: The manual warns that crossing grooves or gratings at an angle forces riders to zigzag to stay in the lane, and that the zigzag is far more hazardous than the wandering feeling produced by riding straight across.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.33, 'Grooves and Gratings'
